newsitem.title: UK: The yen, is it fairly valued, too high or too low?.
newsitem.headline: The yen, is it fairly valued, too high or too low?.

text.p: Background fears in the foreign exchange market about possible Bank of Japan intervention to support the sagging yen beg the question as to whether the currency is fairly valued or not.
On Friday, Japanese cabinet minister Kabun Muto said there was nothing wrong with dollar/yen moving above 125 yen and in terms of purchasing power parity 150 yen might be more appropriate.

Although consumer goods in Japan are clearly expensive -- this reporter recently paid 1000 yen (around $8.00 or 5.0 sterling) for a beer in Tokyo -- there are two sets of prices that must be considered, export prices and consumer prices.
The two are very different.

"There is no doubt Japanese manufacturers are very competitive and fully able to cope with dollar/yen around current levels and indeed stronger," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.
"One of the problems with looking at consumer prices is that the Japanese economy has not been fully deregulated."
Deregulation has started to open Japan up to foreign competition and that has forced retailers, wholesalers and producers to cut prices.
The cost of living in Japan is still high but further deregulation will mean that the consumer price level can come down further.
"It's deregulation that is distorting the PPP picture, more deregulation will see PPP down to around more sensible levels," Lyons said.
In fact, one reason that some sectors of the Japanese stock market have not done well is because further deregulation will make greater inroads into profit margins.

On the export side of the price equation the restructuring that took place when the yen was soaring during 1994 and into 1995 saw industry redouble its cost cutting efforts by paring both labour and non-labour costs.

"You are on fairly safe ground saying that firms make money with the dollar at 110 yen and with it well through 120 they must be minting it," said Ian Harwood, International Economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
"Prices are indicative of the dualistic nature of the Japanese economy with a pretty competitive export sector and even now a fairly highly regulated domestic sector."
Analysts noted that last November Honda moved production of one model back to Tokyo and Toyota announced that its new stationwagon would be produced in Japan.
Both because the motor industry is happy to keep production at home if the yen is weaker than anything around 100 to 110 per dollar.
So if Japanese industry is more than happy with dollar/yen around current levels why the talk of intervention?
There are several reasons, not the least of which is concern that the longer dollar/yen remains at a relatively high level, the more likely it is to decline significantly when it does snap back.

"The economy is recovering and Japan now believes that the exchange rate is no longer reflecting the economic fundamentals but is reflecting a set of perceptions that are probably misplaced," said Chris Tinker, Chief Treasury Economist at Standard Chartered.
The authorities also know that Japanese investors have big exposure overseas and what they do not want is for them to get stung if dollar/yen snaps back to 115.

On top of this there is an element of international co-operation and with a burgeoning trade surplus in Japan any move higher would upset the U.S., where the auto industry has already voiced concern about their lack of competitiveness.
"The nature of the market has been driven by fundamentals but it's now being driven by speculators and they want to get the speculative froth out of the market," Tinker added.
"I think 120 dollar/yen is what the Bank of Japan would be fine with, industry would be fine with and the Americans would probably be fine with."
"But the reality is that if it looks like going to 120 it will probably end up going to 115," he warned.
